item.title: Dutch inflation hits 3.7%, analysts fear more after US midterms
item.description:
Dutch inflation hits 3.7%, analysts fear more after US midterms

November 4, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Inflation in the Netherlands rose to 3.7% in October from 3.4% in September, mainly because of higher energy and fuel prices, which analysts fear will go higher if the Middle East conflict escalates following the US midterm election results.

Energy prices, including petrol and diesel, were 14.4% higher than a year earlier, according to the first estimate by national statistics office CBS.

It is the highest rate since April 2025, when inflation stood at 4.1%. It is also the fourth monthly rise in a row.

Analysts quoted by the Financieele Dagblad expect inflation to rise further after the Democrats’ landslide victory in Tuesday’s US midterm elections.

Thomas van Galen, chief strategist at Achmea Investment Management, told the paper he expects president Donald Trump to focus more on foreign policy, including the war in Iran. “Think of more sabre-rattling in the Middle East,” he said.

Rabobank’s base scenario has oil reaching $120 a barrel in the first half of 2027, economist Igor Dzambo told the FD. On that scenario, a litre of petrol would cost €2.64 on average in March. Rabobank expects inflation to peak at 4.6% just before summer 2027.

item.title: Dutch consumers warned not to buy recalled French condoms
item.description:
Dutch consumers warned not to buy recalled French condoms

November 3, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch health authorities have warned people not to buy French condom brands online that have been recalled because of concerns that they tear too easily.

The French government ordered a recall of seven million prophylactics sold under 10 different brand names across the EU.

The ultra-thin products were manufactured in Malaysia by Richter Robber Technology, but French authorities found discrepancies in the quality and thickness of the latex, breaching safety regulations.

The labels range from big brands to smaller producers that make fair trade or sustainable condoms and include Vitalis, Einhorn, ON and Joy Division.

The healthcare and youth care inspectorate IGJ warned consumers and importers not to buy the condoms because of the risk of spreading STIs. It said it would wait to see if further measures were necessary to prevent them being sold illegally.

French and Dutch authorities have advised anyone who has used the condoms to have themselves tested for STIs. Women should take pregnancy tests if their period is late.

The full list is available on the French government’s website for recalled products, Rappel.

item.title: Philips settles sleep apnoea case with US regulators for €288m
item.description:
Philips settles sleep apnoea case with US regulators for €288m

November 3, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Health technology giant Philips has paid the US justice department €288 million to settle a long-running lawsuit over its defective sleep apnoea devices.

The Amsterdam-based company included the figure in its quarterly results, which also showed the company’s orders and turnovers growing strongly even though its profits dropped sharply.

CEO Roy Jakobs said the agreement in principle with the US government drew a line under the problems with its Respironics machines.

He said it was a “very important step” that would allow Philips to “get back to focusing on innovation”.

The company had to recall 5.5 million machines and 17 million sleep masks worldwide after it emerged that tiny foam particles could be released during cleaning and then inhaled.

Suppressed reports

US regulators started legal action after Philips was found to have suppressed complaints from customers and reports warning it about the risk of using polyster foam in its masks for five years before it began recalling the machines in 2021.

The company also settled a mass claim by users, some of whom said the foam particles had caused lung and nasal cancer, for €1.1 billion two years ago. Philips did not admit liability for the patients’ health problems.

Philips saw its group sales grow by 3% in the third quarter to €4.4 billion. Profits dropped from €187 million to €28 million, partly reflecting the settlement of the sleep apnoea cases.

In the previous quarter the company posted a €186 million windfall in tariffs repaid by the Trump administration after the United States Supreme Court ruled they had been levied illegally.

Jakobs said Philips was reaping the fruits of investing in AI to make medical devices smarter and more efficient.

AI robots had cut the time for MRI scans to be halved, allowing hospitals to scan more patients in a day and cut waiting lists, the CEO said. “It’s great for the patient and the hospital to reduce the waiting list so that they can now help twice as many people for the same cost.”

item.title: Firework sellers fuming over damp squib compensation plan
item.description:
Firework sellers fuming over damp squib compensation plan

November 3, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Fireworks shops are not happy after being told they can claim compensation for lost income ahead of the upcoming ban on fireworks set for New Year’s Eve.

Retailers were told they’re entitled to compensation for lost profit if they sold fireworks for last New Year’s Eve and in at least one December before that. The payout will be based on how much stock they bought in a previous year.

National fireworks foundation Vuurwerkcheck has branded the compensation scheme “as limited as possible”, and reemphasised that it believes the ban will only fuel the trade in black market fireworks, which are often far more powerful and dangerous.

Frans Köhler, chairman of the foundation, said that retailers who rely on winter sales are heading for bankruptcy, and that some have to adapt their businesses to sell other produce, and were given only one year to do so. The cost of those adaptations will be far higher than the compensation, he told broadcaster NOS.

In April 2025, a parliamentary majority voted in favour of a total ban on consumer fireworks. The Senate also voted in favour in July that year, and the law came into force this August.

High powered fireworks, often obtained illegally abroad, cause serious injuries and damage each year. Last New Year’s Eve, 1,239 people were treated for fireworks injuries at A&E departments or out-of-hours GP posts, up 7% on the year before, according to safety institute VeiligheidNL.

At the last turn of the year, it is suspected that a firework may have burned down the 19th-century Vondelkerk in Amsterdam, though not enough forensic evidence could be found to prove this.

item.title: Why renting outside the big cities is the smart move in 2026
item.description:
Partner content

Why renting outside the big cities is the smart move in 2026

November 3, 2026

Moving to the Netherlands for work usually means aiming for one of the big five cities, but in 2026 the smarter search may start just outside them. Supply in the Dutch private rental sector has been shrinking for a couple of years now, and roughly 42% of unregulated listings now ask more than €2,000 a month, up from 36.5% a year ago, according to Pararius.

That pressure is heaviest exactly where most international jobs are: Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Utrecht, The Hague, and Eindhoven, the so-called G5. Competing directly for a place in one of those cities has become harder. Living just outside them often hasn’t.

That’s mostly down to the trains. The Netherlands is small and its rail network is dense, so a city 15 or 20 minutes down the line by Intercity isn’t really a compromise; it’s closer to a different neighbourhood with better rent.

Here’s where to look around each of the five.
Around Amsterdam, Haarlem is 15 minutes from Amsterdam Centraal and has its own historic centre rather than feeling like an overflow suburb. Amstelveen has direct tram links to the city and tends to suit families looking for more space. Almere, a little further out at about 20 minutes, offers newer, better-insulated housing at a noticeably lower price per square metre. It’s worth comparing current listings of apartments in Amsterdam to get a sense of the price gap.

Between Rotterdam and The Hague, the two cities are close enough together to be linked by both regular trains and the RandstadRail light rail network, which makes the towns in between especially practical. Delft, a canal city almost exactly halfway between the two, and Schiedam, known for its old distilleries and comparatively roomy housing, are both a short train ride from either city. Either lets you keep both cities’ job markets within reach. See what’s listed under apartments in Rotterdam and apartments in The Hague for comparison.

Around Utrecht, the city’s position as the country’s rail hub makes its satellites unusually convenient. Amersfoort, a 15-minute ride away, has a medieval centre and rents that run well below Utrecht’s own. Zeist and Nieuwegein are quieter and greener, and popular with families for exactly that reason. Current listings of apartments in Utrecht are a useful baseline for comparison.

Around Eindhoven, the Brainport tech region stretches well past the city itself. Veldhoven, home to ASML’s headquarters, Best, and Helmond are all tied into the regional transit network and offer a shorter, often bike-friendly commute straight to the tech campuses. Have a look at apartments in Eindhoven to see how the core city compares.

The financial case is fairly straightforward. Amsterdam averages €28.53 per square metre a month, according to the latest Pararius Huurmonitor. A place like Almere or Amersfoort runs considerably lower, which in practice means a two-bedroom home for roughly what a studio costs centrally. Newer buildings in these satellite towns also tend to carry better energy labels, which can shave €100 to €200 off monthly utility bills compared with an older, poorly insulated city-centre flat. And since most Dutch employers reimburse commuting costs, often tax-free, the extra travel is frequently close to free in practice.

What this means for your search
Before signing anywhere outside the city you work in, run the door-to-door commute through the NS journey planner at the times you’d actually travel, and check with your employer how commuting costs are reimbursed, since arrangements vary. The energy label on a listing is a good early indicator of what your monthly bills will look like.

The usual paperwork still applies outside the big cities: landlords generally expect a gross income of three to four times the monthly rent, so have your employment contract, recent payslips, and a short rental history ready before you apply. Pararius only lists properties from verified, professional agents, and the satellite towns sit right alongside the cities in its search.

You can view all listings here.

item.title: Jetten hopes sweeteners will win opposition backing for budget
item.description:
Jetten hopes sweeteners will win opposition backing for budget

November 3, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The cabinet looks set to take its budget for 2027 to the brink after failing to secure support from opposition parties ahead of the crucial votes on the plans next week.

Prime minister Rob Jetten called on opposition parties to “take responsibility” when the budget plans are debated on Wednesday in parliament, where the centre-right coalition is 10 seats short of a majority.

The latest version of the budget includes around €350 million worth of sweeteners to ease the cost of living and address the priorities of parties on the left and right. But both sides say the measures do not go far enough.

The cabinet has abandoned plans for the so-called “tulip tax”, which would have seen VAT on bulbs raised from 9% to 21%, which was a sticking point for the farmers’ party BBB.

Other spending announcements include an extra €10 million to support sustainability measures in agriculture – a demand of the orthodox Protestant party SGP, which has strong support in rural areas, and €15 million for the police and prosecution service.

The latter is a concession to the far-right splinter group of former PVV MPs led by Gidi Markuszower.

No advance deals

Neither the left-wing opposition block of Pro and Volt nor the right-wing alliance of JA21, SGP and BBB were able to negotiate a deal to secure their support for the budget package.

Instead, the cabinet has opted for a riskier pick-and-mix approach of offering concessions to both sides, in the hope that it can attract enough votes from smaller parties to steer the budget through.

The coalition parties are hopeful they can get the support of a third block comprising the ChristenUnie, 50Plus and Markuszower’s group, who between them have 11 seats in the Lower House.

“I am convinced that we can get the House over the line to support these plans,” Jetten told reporters on Monday.

“We have a responsibility here in The Hague to do good things, and that includes a good tax plan with plenty of improvements for citizens and businesses.”

But in the Senate, the coalition will need to find the support of either Pro on the left or the BBB on the right. The former want to raise taxes on the rich while the BBB are pressing the government to tear up its plans to cut nitrogen pollution from livestock farms.

Box 3 reforms

Jetten and finance minister Eelco Heinen also negotiated a compromise on the “box 3” income tax plan, which has been one of the stumbling blocks in the negotiations, during an extra cabinet meeting on Monday evening.

Heinen’s party, the right-wing liberal VVD, wants to replace the taxes on assets in box 3 with a capital gains tax. But the party was not prepared to accept Pro and Volt’s demand to make up the shortfall during the transition period by raising the tax rate for investors.

The Council of State, the government’s constitutional advisory body, weighed in on Monday with a scathing report on the Box 3 reforms, calling the timetable for implementing them “irresponsible”.

Heinen had wanted to switch to a capital gains tax for real estate assets and investments in start-up businesses in 2028 prior to a full changeover in 2030.

The Council of State said the government would have to hire 250 extra staff to administer the new system, at a cost of €31 million, and the tax office would not be able to meet the 2028 deadline.

The cabinet has now delayed the temporary system until 2029, against the Council of State’s recommendation to wait until 2030, which would cost the government more money.

item.title: Get help with careers, homes and more at IamExpat Fair The Hague
item.description:
Partner content

Get help with careers, homes and more at IamExpat Fair The Hague

November 3, 2026

The IamExpat Fair is returning to the Grote Kerk in The Hague on Saturday November 7 with more exhibitors than ever, three international centres from across South Holland and large sections for families and health.

The IamExpat Fair, now in its 24th edition, provides advice and services of all kinds for the international community, from housing and careers to schooling and leisure, including special offers only available for attendees. Tickets go for €6 online, or €10 at the door.

“We have an exciting lineup of exhibitors and workshops this year in The Hague,” says events manager Claire Leunissen.

“From exhibitors specialised in preparing newcomers for the inburgering exams, to career coaches experienced in advising expats, and stocking the health & leisure section with physical and mental resources, we’re confident that services at the IamExpat Fair will help internationals thrive. ”

Workshops, presentations and centres
Experts will run workshops throughout the day on topics including buying a house and securing a mortgage, job hunting and help with lifestyle and health. Places are limited, so make sure to book your chosen sessions in advance – you can sign up here.

The Hague International Centre will have a large stand, joined by representatives from across the province, including Leiden International Centre and the Rotterdam International Center, to answer practical questions about settling in the region.

Learning Dutch and finding work
For newcomers working toward the inburgering exams, there are resources from Inburgering Online and Easy Dutch, alongside language schools including Language Institute Regina Coeli, and Bart de Pau.

Career stands and coaches include recruitment agency Undutchables and Work & Worth Coaching, while Work in South Holland will explain the state of the labour market across the region’s main industries.

Families and health
The Family & Kids section brings together several international schools, including the International School of The Hague, The British School in the Netherlands, International School Delft and Optimist International School. There is also kids’ area where families can play games together.

The Health & Leisure section is one of the largest at the fair, with exhibitors ranging from mental health services to dentists and chiropractors.

The IamExpat Fair The Hague takes place in the Grote Kerk on Saturday November 7 from 10am to 5pm. Free tickets are available online while they last; after that, entry costs €6 in advance or €10 at the door. The first 1,000 visitors receive a free tote bag.

item.title: AI pushing more graduates onto benefits, says UWV
item.description:
AI pushing more graduates onto benefits, says UWV

November 3, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The rise of AI is likely contributing to an increase in highly educated people claiming unemployment benefits in the Netherlands, according to benefits agency UWV.

The share of people claiming unemployment benefit (WW) who have an hbo college or university education rose from 30% in the first half of 2022 to 38% this year. The agency says this is partly because more people in the Netherlands are highly educated.

The agency reports a sharp number in claims from programmers and software developers. Reorganisation in IT-driven sectors like banking has also played a role.

Claims from highly educated marketing and advertising staff and market researchers have also risen sharply, which UWV says is “probably” linked to AI taking over tasks.

“We increasingly see technological developments, particularly artificial intelligence, as the cause,” UWV board member Judith Duveen told the Financieele Dagblad. “But part of it is also due to geopolitical uncertainty.”

UWV said it expects financial services to lose more jobs than any other sector in the coming years. Several big banks are cutting support staff, such as anti-money laundering teams, partly through digitalisation and AI. Accountants, junior lawyers, translators, copywriters and customer service staff are also listed as under threat.

The tech sector is still expected to add more jobs than any other sector, the report says, as demand grows for AI advisers and data and security specialists despite some programming work being automated.

On Monday, the Dutch central bank DNB published an analysis which found that a quarter of Dutch workers are in jobs where AI can speed up at least half of their tasks. Hbo and university graduates make up 62% of workers in the most exposed occupations, against 45% of the workforce as a whole. DNB said its measure shows where AI can support or automate tasks, not whether jobs will be lost.

item.title: Dual passports issue continues to plague Dutch-based footballers
item.description:
Dual passports issue continues to plague Dutch-based footballers

November 3, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch-born footballers who were called up to play for former colonies such as Suriname and Indonesia are still in limbo over their national status, six months after the “passportgate” crisis first flared up.

Suriname’s parliament passed a law in September enabling players who are selected for the national team to gain citizenship automatically.

But the Dutch immigration service IND said the law passed in Suriname made no difference to the rules on dual nationality in the Netherlands.

“The fact that Surinamese nationality has been obtained by legal means is not enough on its own to qualify for one of the exceptional categories under our law,” a spokesman for the Dutch justice ministry told broadcaster NOS.

The law was intended to settle the question of dual nationality for footballers, which arose last March when NAC Breda challenged the eligibility of Go Ahead Eagles defender Dean James.

James took Indonesian citizenship last year after accepting an invitation to play for the national team, but under Dutch dual nationality rules he was required to give up his original passport.

KNVB investigation

The Dutch football association KNVB launched an investigation into the employment status of players who were called up by countries such as Suriname, Cape Verde and Indonesia. In the meantime it arranged for Dutch-based players to be given temporary work permits so they could keep playing for their clubs.

Losing Dutch nationality also stripped them of their EU citizenship, meaning they would need to obtain visas and meet stricter criteria, such as an annual salary threshold of €600,000, to be eligible to play in the Eredivisie.

Several players have passed up invitations to join the Surinamese squad because of the uncertainty, including Danilho Doekhi of Lazio, Milan van Ewijk of Coventry City and Jayden Oosterwolde of Fenerbahçe.

National team manager Henk Fraser said it was “inexplicable” that players’ livelihoods were being damaged by their desire to play international football.

“Both countries have to get together and clarify the situation,” he told NOS. “This is a straightforward case of people following their hearts and wanting to play for Suriname, but not knowing where they stand.”

“Sports passports”

Some players said they felt misled by the Surinamese football association, which told them they were playing for the national team on “sports passports” that allowed them to remain Dutch citizens.

Former Feyenoord winger Jean-Paul Boëtius said he only discovered after he was first called up for Suriname last year that he had inadvertently renounced his Dutch citizenship as a result.

Shortly afterwards he received a letter from the city council in Rotterdam telling him to hand in his Dutch passport, which he had recently renewed, because it was no longer valid.

“I now have a sticker in my Surinamese passport that says I have a residency permit allowing me to live in the Netherlands,” he told NOS. “But that’s only for a year. It’s a very difficult situation. I want to become Dutch again. I was born and brought up here.”

item.title: Double shooting in Rotterdam leaves one dead, one injured
item.description:
Double shooting in Rotterdam leaves one dead, one injured

November 3, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

One man has died and another is seriously injured after a shooting in Rotterdam on Monday evening, police have said.

The shooting happened at around 8pm in the Ooosterflank area of the city. While investigations are ongoing, reports say that the victims were in a car, along with two others, when someone opened fire. The driver was killed.

Several ambulances and a trauma helicopter were sent to the scene. Police said they could not yet say what had happened.

The three surviving people in the car fled after the shooting and were arrested shortly after. They are being treated as suspects, including the seriously injured man, broadcaster NOS reported. They are a 60-year-old Rotterdam resident and two men (35 and 54) of no fixed address.
